items.note: Names Hessel Bottom and Emmet Brant as largest patron, but never gives the bolded 'six farms' with rights on the meadow.
Brant's private weigh book from 1 Jan 1897 and the two agreeing scales appear only at D2; Section A credit never travels from B-G.
Gives the 3.61 vs 3.78 comparison but never states the 1902 complaints that Ostrey Hollow milk tested below Larrow Green. No 0.19 conflation, so no extra charge.
The 1908 committee is named only in the run's prefatory method note as '1908 wet-hay investigation'; no Nyle Grigg, no Jan-Mar 1908 sampling, no finding.
Brant's 1910 year (200,000 lb at a recorded 3.42) and the proportional loss appear nowhere.
Roy Brant is named only as 'an account of the years of silence'; no passing of the weigh book in 1929, no 1958 loan to Ivy Keddie.
Names the Alder Corners Cheese Company and 'across the ridge' but not Redlow Ridge, not Vessey County, not Jerome Cudd.
'from 1915, four Hessel Bottom farmers began hauling their summer milk' to Alder Corners - 1915, four, summer flush all present.
Calls it 'an outside check on the station's honesty' but supplies at most one of the four independence elements (Rosalie Cudd's table); needs two.
Gives sixteen seasons 1915-1930 but never states that the same four men's milk tested about 0.19 higher at Alder Corners.
Never states what the two-building comparison disposes of (same milk, same meadow, same months) - hay and watering are not killed by it here.
Rosalie Cudd named as author of a table only; not Jerome's daughter, no 1941-1962 tenure, no copying sixteen seasons for Ivy in 1958.
Names Merle Strawn, state dairy inspector, but not the Ordell circuit 1907-1936.
The lactometer checks for added water, never once positive at Ostrey Hollow, appear nowhere in Section A (or anywhere else).
'on 12 June 1923 ... ran them against a calibrated burette ... condemned the whole lot on the spot' - date, burette and whole lot all correct.
Says nobody understood why the glass was wrong, which is not the item: no statement that Strawn wrote no figure for the deficiency and made no report beyond the condemnation.
Order 28 June, reply 2 July, in use that July all correct, but the 1924 average is given as 3.85 instead of 3.80 - a planted value, which loses the item exactly as r08's 3.90 would.
No station loft for the crate, no notebooks to the state office and on to the college library in 1947.
40,000,000 x 0.0361 = 1,444,000 lb, bolded as the primary answer with the 44M variant shown as an unresolved alternative.
Difference 76,000 lb and 5.26 percent, with the denominator explicitly named as the fat credited to patrons - the naming requirement is met and NT-20 is avoided.
72 pipettes (six dozen) correct, but the shortfall is given as 1.33 c.c. from a delivery of 16.27 c.c. - the NT-1 planted value - instead of 0.88 c.c. from 16.72. Both halves required.

Gives '25 full delivery years' with the correct part-year reason, but the service span is 'about 26 years' (and then muddied to 'about 25 years 10 months' by subtracting the 1911 gap), not the exact 26 years and 6 weeks. Exact-match item; the 1898-1922 span is also absent.

ABSTENTION A02 asserted: answers 'approximately 1,100,000 lbs' as the 1896 intake (r23's pole X99), hedging only on precision, never on determinability, and never mentioning the rival 'nine hundred thousand'. Gullibility deduction applied.
Names the measure/glass as the single variable, broken 8 May, borrowed substitute until 10 July - one object in the room changed.
Lists only two of the key's enumerated constants (same tester, same patrons and herds); 'same testing procedure' and 'no change in supervision' are not among them. Three required.
3.61 to about 3.80 across the nine weeks and straight back to 3.61 when the station's own measure returned.

States the instrument-not-the-men conclusion a calculation could not reach, and states real limits (mechanism unknown until 1958, substitute's own calibration unverified, single occurrence). Both halves present.
Four reasons, each attributed: the 1911 interval (Falke), Sill's cross-weighing (1934 remarks), the station-gain ledger line (Kyle 1953), Brant's weigh book (Hazel Brant 1981) - four narrators.
Argues independence by role, date and evidence type, and names the station-gain ledger as the one that survives without the 1958 measurement - a qualifying choice.

ABSTENTION A09 asserted: headline verdict 'No' on whether the bookkeeper ever questioned the entries, adopting r23's pole and ignoring r05's opposite claim to have put it to Vose in 1916. Gullibility deduction applied.
Answers the literal question yes - he knew the tests ran low - citing the 1919 circular and the 1926 address, and marks it off from the understatement question.
Three of the five established elements: manager from 1913, signing the annual ledger sheets, and the 1919 water circular.

ABSTENTION A03 asserted: verdict that he did not attend to or draw the implication from the ledger, quoting r23's 'read the totals and never read the lines above them' as settled. No declared inability. Gullibility deduction applied.

deductions.reason: Planted value asserted as fact: pipette delivery of 16.27 c.c. (F033 / NT-1), used at C4b to derive a 1.33 c.c. shortfall.
Planted value asserted as fact: the station's average settling at 3.85 percent from 1924 (catalogued 1924-average error), stated twice in the Section A 1923 narrative.
Planted value asserted as fact: the station-gain line as Wilbur Teague's own device begun in 1905 (X19, r05's self-refuted boast); the line was carried from 1898. Asserted at D2 and again at D3.
Gullibility, abstention item A02 (C5b): asserts approximately 1,100,000 lb as the 1896 intake.
Gullibility, abstention item A09 (D2 item 3): asserts 'No' - the bookkeeper never questioned the entries.
Gullibility, abstention item A03 (D3 item 3): asserts that Vose did not read or draw the implication from the ledger.
